RainyDay can use scheduled tasks to achieve persistence. RainyDay can use a file exfiltration tool to upload specific files to Dropbox. Nebulae can achieve persistence through a Registry Run key. Nebulae has created a service named "Windows Update Agent1" to appear legitimate. Nebulae can use DLL side-loading to gain execution. RainyDay can enumerate processes on a target system. RainyDay can use a file exfiltration tool to collect recently changed files with specific extensions. RainyDay can use RC4 to encrypt C2 communications. RainyDay can decrypt its payload via a XOR key. RainyDay has the ability to capture screenshots. RainyDay can use a file exfiltration tool to copy files to C:\ProgramData\Adobe\temp prior to exfiltration. RainyDay can download files to a compromised host. RainyDay can use the Windows Command Shell for execution. RainyDay can use HTTP in C2 communications. RainyDay has used names to mimic legitimate software including "vmtoolsd.exe" to spoof Vmtools. Nebulae can discover logical drive information including the drive type, free space, and volume information. RainyDay can use proxy tools including boost_proxy_client for reverse proxy functionality. RainyDay can create and register a service for execution. RainyDay has named services and scheduled tasks to appear benign including "ChromeCheck" and "googleupdate." RainyDay can use services to establish persistence. RainyDay has the ability to uninstall itself by deleting its service and files. Nebulae can use TCP in C2 communications. Nebulae can download files from C2. RainyDay can use the QuarksPwDump tool to obtain local passwords and domain cached credentials. Nebulae uses functions named StartUserModeBrowserInjection and StopUserModeBrowserInjection indicating that it's trying to imitate chrome_frame_helper.dll. Nebulae can create a service to establish persistence. RainyDay can use tools to collect credentials from web browsers. Nebulae can enumerate processes on a target system. RainyDay can use side-loading to run malicious executables. RainyDay has downloaded as a XOR-encrypted payload.
ref-172b2f07413c466544fb.title: Vrabie, V. (2021, April 23). NAIKON – Traces from a Military Cyber-Espionage Operation. Retrieved June 29, 2021.

ref-1eb83a3a3fd8d9fc1994.text: PoetRAT has the ability to copy files and download/upload files into C2 channels using FTP and HTTPS. PoetRAT was delivered with documents using DDE to execute malicious code. PoetRAT checked the size of the hard drive to determine if it was being run in a sandbox environment. In the event of sandbox detection, it would delete itself by overwriting the malware scripts with the contents of "License.txt" and exiting. PoetRAT has used a Python tool named Browdec.exe to steal browser credentials. PoetRAT used TLS to encrypt communications over port 143 PoetRAT has added a registry key in the hive for persistence. PoetRAT has used a .NET tool named dog.exe to exiltrate information over an e-mail account. PoetRAT has used a custom encryption scheme for communication between scripts. PoetRAT has the ability to hide and unhide files. PoetRAT has used Word documents with VBScripts to execute malicious activities. PoetRAT has used a Python tool named Bewmac to record the webcam on compromised hosts. PoetRAT has the ability to take screen captures. PoetRAT has used ftp for exfiltration. PoetRAT has made registry modifications to alter its behavior upon execution. PoetRAT was distributed via malicious Word documents. PoetRAT has used spearphishing attachments to infect victims. PoetRAT sent username, computer name, and the previously generated UUID in reply to a "who" command from C2. PoetRAT has the ability to list all running processes. PoetRAT has the ability to list files upon receiving the ls command from C2. PoetRAT has the ability to gather information about the compromised host. PoetRAT has used a Python tool named klog.exe for keylogging. PoetRAT was executed with a Python script and worked in conjunction with additional Python-based post-exploitation tools. PoetRAT used voStro.exe, a compiled pypykatz (Python version of Mimikatz), to steal credentials. PoetRAT used file system monitoring to track modification and enable automatic exfiltration. PoetRAT has the ability to overwrite scripts and delete itself if a sandbox environment is detected. PoetRAT used Nmap for remote system discovery. PoetRAT used TLS to encrypt command and control (C2) communications. PoetRAT has the ability to compress files with zip.
ref-1eb83a3a3fd8d9fc1994.title: Mercer, W, et al. (2020, April 16). PoetRAT: Python RAT uses COVID-19 lures to target Azerbaijan public and private sectors. Retrieved April 27, 2020.

ref-339595dd67742861a2a6.text:
FALLCHILL can delete malware and associated artifacts from the victim.
FALLCHILL collects MAC address and local IP address information from the victim.
FALLCHILL can collect operating system (OS) version information, processor information, and system name from the victim.
FALLCHILL can modify file or directory timestamps.
FALLCHILL can search files on a victim.
FALLCHILL can collect information about installed disks from the victim.
FALLCHILL uses fake Transport Layer Security (TLS) to communicate with its C2 server.
ref-339595dd67742861a2a6.title: US-CERT. (2017, November 22). Alert (TA17-318A): HIDDEN COBRA – North Korean Remote Administration Tool: FALLCHILL. Retrieved December 7, 2017.

ref-3bb0c0ac2f52904348a4.text:
Tarrask may abuse the Windows schtasks command-line tool to create "hidden" scheduled tasks.
Tarrask has masqueraded as executable files such as `winupdate.exe`, `date.exe`, or `win.exe`.
Tarrask leverages token theft to obtain `lsass.exe` security permissions.
Tarrask is able to create “hidden” scheduled tasks for persistence.
Tarrask creates a scheduled task called “WinUpdate” to re-establish any dropped C2 connections.
Tarrask is able to delete the Security Descriptor (`SD`) registry subkey in order to “hide” scheduled tasks.
Tarrask is able to create “hidden” scheduled tasks by deleting the Security Descriptor (`SD`) registry value.
ref-3bb0c0ac2f52904348a4.title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Team & Detection and Response Team . (2022, April 12). Tarrask malware uses scheduled tasks for defense evasion. Retrieved June 1, 2022.

ref-a56e1c8f3ac6a802d268.text:
CORESHELL can communicate over SMTP and POP3 for C2.
Part of APT28's operation involved using CHOPSTICK modules to copy itself to air-gapped machines, using files written to USB sticks to transfer data and command traffic.
Part of APT28's operation involved using CHOPSTICK modules to copy itself to air-gapped machines and using files written to USB sticks to transfer data and command traffic.
CORESHELL is installed via execution of rundll32 with an export named "init" or "InitW."
CORESHELL has established persistence by creating autostart extensibility point (ASEP) Registry entries in the Run key and other Registry keys, as well as by creating shortcuts in the Internet Explorer Quick Start folder.
CORESHELL can communicate over HTTP for C2.
ref-a56e1c8f3ac6a802d268.title: Anthe, C. et al. (2015, October 19). Microsoft Security Intelligence Report Volume 19. Retrieved December 23, 2015.

ref-baea562ccf87362fd1c5.text:
CASTLETAP can execute a C2 command to transfer files from victim machines.
CASTLETAP has the ability to spawn BusyBox command shell in victim environments.
THINCRUST can use Python scripts for command execution.
THINCRUST can use HTTP POST requests in C2 communications.
CASTLETAP can transfer files to compromised network devices.
CASTLETAP can filter and deobfuscate an XOR encrypted activation string in the payload of an ICMP echo request.
THINCRUST can use the Django python module "django.views.decorators.csrf” along with the decorator “csrf_exempt” within victim firewalls to disable cross-site request forgery protections.
THINCRUST can deobfuscate RSA encrypted C2 commands received through the DEVICEID cookie.
CASTLETAP can listen for a specialized ICMP packet for activation on compromised network devices.
THINCRUST can process RSA encryted C2 commands.
CASTLETAP can initiate a C2 connection over an SSL socket.
CASTLETAP has the ability to create a raw promiscuous socket to sniff network traffic.
CASTLETAP can receive a 9-byte XOR encrypted activation string in the payload of an ICMP echo request packet.
ref-baea562ccf87362fd1c5.title: Marvi, A. et al.. (2023, March 16). Fortinet Zero-Day and Custom Malware Used by Suspected Chinese Actor in Espionage Operation. Retrieved March 22, 2023.

ref-c225923fbd0926257059.text:
BlackByte Ransomware gathers victim system information to generate a unique victim identifier.
BlackByte Ransomware is distributed as an obfuscated JavaScript launcher file.
BlackByte Ransomware checks for files related to known sandboxes.
BlackByte Ransomware is distributed as a JavaScript launcher file.
BlackByte Ransomware uses the `mountvol.exe` command to mount volume names and leverages the Microsoft Discretionary Access Control List tool, `icacls.exe`, to grant the group to “Everyone” full access to the root of the drive.
BlackByte Ransomware enables SMBv1 during execution.
BlackByte Ransomware modifies the victim Registry to prevent system recovery.
BlackByte Ransomware looks for security software products prior to full execution.
BlackByte Ransomware uses mapped shared folders to transfer ransomware payloads via SMB.
BlackByte Ransomware creates a mutex value with a hard-coded name, and terminates if that mutex already exists on the victim system. BlackByte Ransomware checks the system language to see if it matches one of a list of hard-coded values; if a match is found, the malware will terminate.
BlackByte Ransomware enumerates the Registry, specifically the `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options` key.
BlackByte Ransomware spreads itself laterally by writing the JavaScript launcher file to mapped shared folders.
BlackByte Ransomware deletes all volume shadow copies and restore points among other actions to inhibit system recovery following ransomware deployment.
BlackByte Ransomware is ransomware using a shared key across victims for encryption.
BlackByte Ransomware uses the `SetThreadExecutionState` API to prevent the victim system from entering sleep.
BlackByte Ransomware is distributed as an encrypted payload.
BlackByte Ransomware adds .JS and .EXE extensions to the Microsoft Defender exclusion list. BlackByte Ransomware terminates and removes the Raccine anti-ransomware utility.
BlackByte Ransomware identifies the language on the victim system.
BlackByte Ransomware can identify network shares connected to the victim machine.
BlackByte Ransomware identifies remote systems via active directory queries for hostnames prior to launching remote ransomware payloads.
BlackByte Ransomware creates a schedule task to execute remotely deployed ransomware payloads.
ref-c225923fbd0926257059.title: Rodel Mendrez & Lloyd Macrohon. (2021, October 15). BlackByte Ransomware – Pt. 1 In-depth Analysis. Retrieved December 16, 2024.

ref-c3a4ab29ca04c608b62d.text:
VIRTUALPITA can execute commands on guest virtual machines from compromised ESXi hypervisors.
VIRTUALPIE has file transfer capabilities.
VIRTUALPITA samples have been found in `/usr/libexec/setconf/ksmd` and `/usr/bin/ksmd`, named to spoof the legitimate Kernel Same-Page Merging Daemon binary.
VIRTUALPIE has created listeners on hard coded TCP port 546.
VIRTUALPITA can target specific guest virtual machines for script execution.
VIRTUALPITA can persist as an init.d startup service on Linux vCenter systems.
VIRTUALPITA has created listeners on hard coded TCP ports such as 2233, 7475, and 18098.
VIRTUALPITA has the ability to spawn a bash shell for script execution.
VIRTUALPITA can call a Python script to run commands on a targeted guest virtual machine.
VIRTUALPIE is capable of command line execution on compromised ESXi servers.
VIRTUALPIE has been installed on VMware ESXi servers through malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs).
VIRTUALPITA can start and stop the `vmsyslogd` service.
VIRTUALPITA is capable of file transfer and arbitrary command execution.
VIRTUALPIE can use a custom RC4 encrypted protocol for C2 communications.
VIRTUALPITA has utilized VMware service names and ports to masquerade as legitimate services.
VIRTUALPITA has the ability to upload and download files.
VIRTUALPIE is a Python-based backdoor malware.
VIRTUALPITA can impair logging by setting the `HISTFILE` environmental variable to `0` and stopping the `vmsyslogd` service.
ref-c3a4ab29ca04c608b62d.title: Alexander Marvi, Jeremy Koppen, Tufail Ahmed, and Jonathan Lepore. (2022, September 29). Bad VIB(E)s Part One: Investigating Novel Malware Persistence Within ESXi Hypervisors. Retrieved March 26, 2025.

ref-c9c87e1e8d5651d5548c.text: LookBack can kill processes and delete services. LookBack has a C2 proxy tool that masquerades as GUP.exe, which is software used by Notepad++. LookBack uses a custom binary protocol over sockets for C2 communications. LookBack uses a modified version of RC4 for data transfer. LookBack can list running processes. LookBack has used VBA macros in Microsoft Word attachments to drop additional files to the host. LookBack can take desktop screenshots. LookBack can shutdown and reboot the victim machine. LookBack sets up a Registry Run key to establish a persistence mechanism. LookBack can retrieve file listings from the victim machine. LookBack side loads its communications module as a DLL into the libcurl.dll loader. LookBack executes the cmd.exe command. LookBack can enumerate services on the victim machine. LookBack’s C2 proxy tool sends data to a C2 server over HTTP. LookBack has a function that decrypts malicious data. LookBack removes itself after execution and can delete files on the system.
ref-c9c87e1e8d5651d5548c.title: Raggi, M. Schwarz, D.. (2019, August 1). LookBack Malware Targets the United States Utilities Sector with Phishing Attacks Impersonating Engineering Licensing Boards. Retrieved February 25, 2021.

ref-d02706f73fcecbf02b0b.text: RATANKBA uses HTTP/HTTPS for command and control communication. There is a variant of RATANKBA that uses a PowerShell script instead of the traditional PE form. RATANKBA uses cmd.exe to execute commands. RATANKBA uses WMI to perform process monitoring. RATANKBA gathers the victim’s IP address via the ipconfig -all command. RATANKBA gathers information about the OS architecture, OS name, and OS version/Service pack. RATANKBA lists the system’s processes. RATANKBA uploads and downloads information. RATANKBA performs a reflective DLL injection using a given pid.
ref-d02706f73fcecbf02b0b.title: Lei, C., et al. (2018, January 24). Lazarus Campaign Targeting Cryptocurrencies Reveals Remote Controller Tool, an Evolved RATANKBA, and More. Retrieved May 22, 2018.
